style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: ACR Guidelines for Rheumatic Diseases & EULAR Consensus (2024)

clinical_targets.goal: Normalization of serum CRP and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
Halt radiographic joint erosion and preserve physical mobility

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
Step 3: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
Step 4: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Arthritis focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Arthritis.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Arthritis.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Arthritis require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Multidisciplinary tertiary intervention for refractory disease.
drug_classes.pearls: Consult subspecialty guidelines and consider therapeutic drug monitoring where applicable.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Arthritis.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.
Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Avoid NSAIDs in eGFR < 30 mL/min; adjust methotrexate and allopurinol based on renal clearance.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Screen for hepatitis B/C before starting DMARDs or biologics; monitor ALT/AST with methotrexate.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Methotrexate and leflunomide are strictly contraindicated; certolizumab and hydroxychloroquine are preferred.
special_populations.elderly: High risk of NSAID-induced gastrointestinal ulcers, fluid retention, and acute kidney injury; co-prescribe PPI.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is arthritis? If you feel pain and stiffness in your body or have trouble moving around, you might have arthritis. Any disorder that affects the joints is often called arthritis. Joints are places where two bones meet, such as your elbow or knee. Most types of arthritis can cause joint pain and inflammation (swelling). Over time, a swollen joint can become severely damaged. Some kinds of arthritis can also cause problems in your organs, such as your eyes or skin. Treatment will depend on the type of arthritis you have. What are the types of arthritis? Common types of arthritis include: Osteoarthritis is the most common type of arthritis. It's often related to aging or injury. Autoimmune arthritis happens when your body's immune system attacks healthy cells in your body by mistake. Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common form of this type of arthritis. Juvenile arthritis is a type of arthritis that happens in children. Infectious arthritis is an infection that has spread from another part of your body to the joint. Reactive arthritis is one type. Psoriatic arthritis affects people with psoriasis (itchy or sore scaly red and white skin patches). Gout is a painful type of arthritis that happens when too much uric acid builds up in your body. It often starts in the big toe. Other joints can also be affected. Ankylosing spondylitis is a type of arthritis of the spine that can cause stiffness and make it difficult to move and bend. What are the symptoms of arthritis? Pain, redness, warmth, and joint inflammation are common arthritis symptoms. You may not be able to move your joint as well as it should. Other symptoms could include fever , weight loss, breathing difficulties, or a rash. Symptoms often get worse as you age. Some symptoms of arthritis may be signs of other illnesses. Who is more likely to get arthritis? A few things that might increase your chance of getting arthritis include: Family history. You may be more likely to get certain types of arthritis if a member of your family has the disorder. Age. The risk of getting many types of arthritis increases with age. Sex. Certain types of arthritis are more common in women, while other types are more common in men. Other factors that might increase your risk of getting arthritis include having a previous joint injury, obesity , or lupus . How is arthritis diagnosed? To find out if you have arthritis, your health care provider may: Ask you about your medical history, including your symptoms. Do a physical exam. Order blood tests or take x-rays . Your provider may refer you to a rheumatologist (a doctor who specializes in arthritis care) for tests, diagnosis, and care. What are the treatments for arthritis? Treatment depends on the type of arthritis you have. It may include medicine or surgery. Your provider will work with you to improve your symptoms and quality of life. A few ways to help manage your symptoms include: Hot or cold packs Relaxation techniques Use of splints, braces, and/or assistive devices NIH: National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases
style_3_monograph.treatment: The goal of treatment for adult Still disease is to control the symptoms of arthritis . Aspirin and other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), such as ibuprofen, are most often used first. Prednisone may be used for more severe cases. If the disease is severe or persists for a long time (becomes chronic), medicines that suppress the immune system might be needed. Such medicines include: Methotrexate Anakinra (interleukin-1 receptor agonist) Tocilizumab (interleukin 6 inhibitor) Tumor necrosis factor (TNF) antagonists such as etanercept (Enbrel)
